A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00554

In Islam in Modern History, Wilfred Cantwell Smith does justice to this question in an illuminating comparison between Islamic and Marxist approaches to history. Both Islam and Marxism, he says, attach great importance to the way history unfolds. Neither sees historical events as random occurrences. Both believe that these events follow a certain course, that the course has meaning, and that we can draw from it certain patterns — what the Quran calls God's established ways, or what Marxism calls the laws of history. But here is the difference: Marxism sees only one meaning in a historical event, a purely material one. Islam sees two: one material, belonging to this world, and one spiritual, belonging to the world to come.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00555

If we return to the Quran, we find that its accounts of the missions of the prophets and messengers leave aside the small details and personal circumstances to focus on the overall direction of events and the lesson to be learnt. The missions of the messengers, as the Quran describes them, were far from simple or easy. They all met with ridicule and rejection. Certain forces therefore set themselves against the messengers and the justice and freedom they sought to bring about. The messengers had to press on with their cause and continue their struggle in the face of these opposing forces. The Quran describes them as follows:
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00556
First. Kings and tyrants, as we see in its references to Pharaoh, Qarun and Haman, among others.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00557
Second. The rich and those who live in luxury, as the Quran tells us:
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00558

“Whenever We sent a warner to a town, its wealthy people said, ‘We reject the message you have brought.’ They said, ‘We have more wealth and children, and we shall not be punished.’ Say, ‘My Lord gives generously to whom He wills and restricts His gifts to whom He wills, but most people do not know.’”
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00559

Third. The reactionaries, whom the Quran describes as those who cling to the ways of their fathers and grandfathers. “In the same way, whenever We sent a warner before you to a town, its wealthy people said, ‘We found our fathers following a way of life, and we are following in their footsteps.’”
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00560

Fourth. The followers of the powerful, and the downtrodden whose interests would actually be served by supporting the cause. Instead, they stand against it, siding with the masters and leading figures they serve and from whom they seek honour. How vividly the Quran portrays the position of these oppressed people when they and their masters face God on the Day of Judgement and try to escape responsibility for their submission and their crimes! “They will say, ‘Our Lord, we obeyed our masters and our leaders, and they led us astray.’” But no excuse will be accepted for putting up with humiliation and helping tyrants in their oppression. Instead, they will be asked on the Day of Judgement, “Was God's earth not wide enough for you to move elsewhere?”
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00561

Fifth. Those who fritter away their time, amuse themselves and follow their whims; those who “buy idle talk” and “argue about God without knowledge, guidance or an enlightening scripture”. In today's language, this applies to people who make a hobby of debate and intellectual quarrels but have no intention of contributing any serious work.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00562
As for the groups that supported and stood by the messengers, the Quran describes them as follows:
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00563

First. The vast majority of the people who were powerless, humiliated and exploited. The enemies of the messengers called them the lowest of the low, the rabble and the slaves, as we see in the struggles of Noah, Muhammad and Jesus.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00564

Second. A select group of free citizens who stood for progress. In modern language, they were rather like the leading ranks of a revolutionary movement. Think of the disciples in the story of Jesus and the Companions in the struggle of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00565

This careful analysis of the social classes that supported the messengers and those that opposed them brings out the human reality of class conflict. It arises from clashes of interest, but it does not operate as a law that inevitably demands bloodshed and violence in every case.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00566

These missions, with the struggles that accompanied them and ran through them, always came to an inevitable conclusion. Either the cause triumphed or it could no longer hold out, and God poured out His wrath upon the wrongdoers through disasters of nature — storms, hurricanes, earthquakes, floods and the like. God, having left human beings free to choose, did not wish to make all people a single community. He would reward or punish them according to their deeds. The Quran calls this inevitable outcome a sunna, an unchanging law: “Such was God's way with those who passed away before, and God's command is a decree ordained.” It makes the point repeatedly in other verses: “You will find no change in God's way.”
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00567

All this makes it quite clear that if we want to establish the roots of our socialist thought, our first recourse must be the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet. When we turn to them, we find that Islam brought forth a theory of socialism long before Marxism set about formulating such a theory in modern economics.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00568

At its heart, the Islamic theory guarantees everyone a decent and dignified share in life. In the language of modern economics, it guarantees an adequate standard of living based on equal opportunities and a shared enjoyment of nature's bounty and the fruits of science and civilisation. Everyone is free to earn more than this minimum through their own hard work, without exploiting the labour of others. Naturally, this means that people will have different levels of income. But these differences are not left to grow without limit. There is a ceiling, a safeguard against their hardening into distinct social classes. Islam therefore imposes a maximum income to stop wealth accumulating in the hands of a few to the point where a class system threatens to emerge.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00569

In short, the aim of Islamic socialism is to build a classless society in which work is the foundation of a citizen's social worth and the measure of it. People earn different amounts according to their work, within a range between a minimum and a maximum standard of living. As development projects increase production and national income, we can narrow that range. In other words, greater or sufficient production leads to a fairer distribution of wealth. This is why we have our own name for a socialist society: a society of sufficiency and justice. Only a ceiling on income can guarantee that we achieve this goal, because it is the practical means of ensuring that greater production goes hand in hand with fairer distribution.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00570

If Islam does not specify what that ceiling should be, it is because it is relative: it varies from place to place and from age to age. The ruler must therefore set it in keeping with the circumstances of society and the changes of the times. This is not a matter of unrestricted personal judgement, however. Four principles laid down in the Quran govern the decision:
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00571

First. Wealth must not be allowed to accumulate in the hands of a few rich people to the point where they can use it to dominate economic and social life and oppress others. “So that wealth does not circulate only among the rich among you.”
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00572

Second. Nor should wealth accumulate in their hands to the point where they plunge into luxury and ever more extravagant displays of status. Society soon begins to disintegrate, corruption spreads, and eventually it collapses altogether. That is the lesson of the fall of the Roman Empire and the collapse of Arab rule in Andalusia, among others. The Quran draws attention to this lesson: “When We wish to destroy a town, We give commands to those who live in luxury there, but they defy them. The sentence against it then becomes due, and We destroy it utterly.”
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00573

Third. Suppose that wealth accumulates in the hands of certain individuals who are neither given to luxury nor concerned with status, and have no wish to dominate or control others. Even then, amassing money for its own sake — hoarding it — runs counter to the interests of the community, because it holds money back from the flow of economic activity. This is the wisdom behind Islam's prohibition of hoarding: “Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God, give them news of a painful punishment.”
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00574

Fourth. Individuals must not accumulate wealth at the expense of other people's rights. Workers must not be cheated out of their wages, nor consumers forced to pay exorbitant prices by those who have a monopoly on the market. The Quran states this principle clearly: “Do not deprive people of what is rightfully theirs, and do not spread corruption throughout the land.”
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00575

These four principles, which guide rulers in setting an upper limit on income in any society and in any age, act naturally as a safeguard against the rise of an exploiting, dominant class. In such a classless society, people would be, as the Prophet said, “equal as the teeth of a comb”, even though their incomes varied.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00576

Islam, then, provided the foundations of a scientific theory of socialism. If we are serious about developing socialist thought rooted in our own heritage, we ought to devote more attention to studying these foundations than to studying the life of Abu Dharr al-Ghifari or uprisings such as those of the Zanj and the Qarmatians in southern Iraq and the Gulf. As I explained in the second part of my book The Development of Socialist Thought, these uprisings or revolutions were not founded on a body of ideas that could be studied as part of the history of socialist thought. For the most part, they were simply spontaneous revolts against exploitation and tyranny. If they show us anything, it is that the seeds of an awakening lay within a sick society. Unfortunately, those seeds produced only confused efforts that failed to bring back the Islamic socialist system as it had been practised under the Prophet [peace and blessings be upon him] and his two great successors, Abu Bakr and Umar. It is even possible that some of these stirrings of an awakening made the illness worse rather than curing it. We see this in the Qarmatian revolt, with its elements that contradicted and departed from Islam.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00577

During that golden age of the Prophet, Islamic socialism was practised through direct democracy. Rulers had neither the trappings of power nor the privileges of an official elite. The Prophet and his two successors ran the affairs of the state from the mosque in Medina, without establishing palaces of government or official institutions inclined towards control and privilege.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00578

But Islam soon suffered a serious setback that gradually took it away from its socialist character. The system of bay'a — pledging allegiance to a ruler through popular consultation and election — gave way to hereditary rule. Muslim rulers and their supporters became ruling families. Throughout the Middle Ages, they formed a privileged class that lived in luxury, surrounded itself with displays of wealth, status and distinction, and cut itself off from the mass of the people. How different this was from the simple life the Prophet and the Rightly Guided Caliphs had lived among ordinary people!
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00579

Some writers take the cause championed by Abu Dharr al-Ghifari as a living example of the socialist movement. In reality, it was above all a sincere stand against this dangerous change when its first signs began to appear under Uthman. It was the first attempt to warn of the impending setback and prevent it. But the forces behind that setback had already begun to emerge and spread, as the Islamic state expanded, wealth poured in from conquest, and contact with the Romans and the West brought the influence of their systems of government. Umar ibn al-Khattab had the insight to recognise the danger of allowing these forces to gather and grow. He firmly restrained the desire for special privileges among the governors of the provinces and their sons. He also forbade the building of grand seats of government like those of the Romans and Persians, and even demolished some of them to ward off the causes of discord.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00580

The forces behind this setback grew stronger under both the Umayyads and the Abbasids. It was only natural that popular uprisings should occur under both dynasties. But in studying these uprisings we must make a distinction. Were they impulsive reactions, marked above all by the immaturity of their revolutionary spirit? Or were they serious and sincere efforts to revive the Islamic system as practised under the Prophet and the Rightly Guided Caliphs?
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00581

Personally, I have no objection whatsoever to our modern historians studying and analysing these uprisings. I sincerely hope, however, that they will remain objective in what they write and avoid reading more into events than the evidence can bear. What matters to me is that we bring out the originality of our own thought. We should not simply label certain popular uprisings in Islamic history as socialist movements ahead of their time, and then find ourselves analysing and judging them in the language of our own age. I am not singling out any particular book or historian. I am warning against a method of research that carries within it more chances of getting things wrong than of getting them right. May God guide us to success.
A Modern Approach Must Not Come at the Expense of Authenticity
passage-en-00582
We responded to Abd al-Mughni Sa'id's views in an article entitled:
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00583
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00584
Here is the text:
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00585

Abd al-Mughni Sa'id has spared us the need to defend the modern historian's right to look at Islamic history through the lens of society. We are delighted that he has joined the discussion as a third voice, in a spirit of fairness and objectivity.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00586

I have known his generosity of spirit and breadth of mind ever since I was a university student regularly attending the Naji Seminar, which he ran in the early sixties. I hope, then, that he will allow me to disagree with him on a central point in his article. He argues that the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet contain a “scientific theory of socialism”, and that Islam offers an approach to historical research which “sees two meanings in historical events, one material and worldly, the other spiritual and relating to the life to come”.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00587

Let me make clear from the outset that our disagreement is not fundamental. I am not denying Islam's socialist character, nor am I belittling the value of its view of history. But I believe that neither the socialist thought in Islam nor the historical accounts in the Quran come to us in the form of a theory of socialism or a method of historical research. What the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet give us in this regard are general principles. To put it simply, Islam contains the spirit of the theory, not the theory itself; the essence of the method, not the method itself.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00588

This in no way detracts from the authenticity of the Quran. On the contrary, it confirms it. Indeed, it is one of the signs of its miraculous nature, alongside others. The Quran gives humanity general principles aimed at the good of humankind in every aspect of political , economic and intellectual life. The word of God is far above being a collection of specific philosophical theories. It is broader and higher than that. In the language of philosophy, we might say that the supreme active intellect laid down the general principles and left it to the receptive intellect — the human mind, the greatest thing God created in His greatest creation, the human being — to formulate theories and devise methods.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00589

The human mind can get things right, and it can get them wrong. No theory explaining the phenomena of the universe is guaranteed to last for ever. What reason establishes, reason can also overturn. The survival of a theory depends on how well it grasps the laws of change. As circumstances change, theories are revised or fade away, making room for others that better fit the new reality. General principles, on the other hand, remain. They are broad and rich enough to embrace theories and methods without being confined by them.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00590

Few Islamic thinkers have grasped this miraculous aspect of the Quran. Most have either clung to the literal wording of the texts, bringing Islamic thought to a standstill, or taken interpretation to such extremes that they lost their bearings. Radically conservative thinkers and extreme liberals arrived at the same result: both overlooked, or chose to overlook, the true relationship between the divine intellect and the human mind.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00591

The Mu'tazilites tried to deepen their understanding of that relationship by freeing the human mind from its chains. But traditionalism was the dominant current. They exhausted their energies in breaking down reactionary rules of thought and restraining the excesses of the liberal current. In the ensuing struggle, traditionalism prevailed, represented by the Ash'arites and the Hanbalites and reaching its height with al-Ghazali. The voice of Ibn Rushd — the voice of reason — was drowned out in the clamour of traditionalism, which grew stronger in the hands of Sufis such as Ibn Arabi and Ibn Sab'in. Sufism turned into a form of unthinking dervish devotion that remained the cornerstone of Islamic thought until the dawn of the modern age. Here lie the real causes of the setback that befell the Islamic world. And here, too, lie the reasons for the European Renaissance, which picked up the thread Ibn Rushd had left behind.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00592

The Quran, then, can inspire modern theories and methods. If dialectics — the study of change and the forces at work within it — is one of the most significant advances modern science has made in explaining the phenomena of the universe and discovering the laws of its movement, I believe that a Muslim philosopher such as Ibn Khaldun recognised its importance long before Hegel astonished the world with his discovery. Consider what Ibn Khaldun wrote in his Muqaddima:
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00593

“One of the subtle mistakes historians make is to forget that the circumstances of nations and generations change as the ages change and the days pass. When people acquire royal power and take control of a state, they inevitably fall back on the customs of their predecessors and adopt many of them, without forgetting the customs of their own generation. The customs of the state thus differ somewhat from those of the first generation. When another state succeeds them, it blends their customs with its own and introduces further changes, departing still more from the first state's ways. This gradual process of change continues until there is a complete difference between the two.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00594

Does that passage not sum up the movement of history and uncover its laws before Hegel discovered them and Marx built the foundations of dialectical materialism upon them? This is why I say that a modern approach strengthens our heritage rather than diminishing it.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00595

Is democracy, the very heart of modern political theory, not what the Quran called for in the principle — not the theory — of shura, or consultation? If the Quran and the sayings of the Prophet contained a theory of government, why did the Prophet not recommend it (peace and blessings be upon him) before his death? The greatness of Islam, then, lies in the fact that it did not hand down theories or devise fixed methods. Instead, it established broad principles and values within which Muslims could shape their systems of government and politics to meet the needs of their own times.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00596

On economic matters, I agree with all Abd al-Mughni Sa'id's thinking about socialism in Islam. Our only disagreement is over his claim that there is an “Islamic scientific theory of socialism”. I too believe that the Quran contains noble principles of social justice, and that from them we can develop a theory not very different from modern scientific socialism. Islam and scientific socialism start from the same point in identifying what stands in the way of justice. The cause lies in human nature, in our love of power and our craving to dominate. God says: “When harm touches him, he is distraught, and when good comes his way, he is withholding.” And He says: “The soul is ever inclined towards evil.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00597

Give free rein to the urge to possess and dominate, and the result is social injustice. A minority exploits the resources of the whole community. And this injustice is of human making: God does not wrong people in the least; it is people who wrong themselves.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00598

The oppressive minority defies what is right: “When We wish to destroy a town, We give commands to those who live in luxury there, but they defy them.” Conflict between the wealthy minority and the masses of the oppressed is inevitable. Islam urges the oppressed to rise up. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “Whoever among you sees a wrong, let him change it...” And God knows that wrongdoers are not deterred by kindness: “We destroyed generations before you when they committed injustice. Their messengers brought them clear proofs, but they would not believe.” It takes force and severity to deter them, and the outcome necessarily favours the oppressed: “We wished to show favour to those who were oppressed in the land, to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors...” These clear verses and others testify to the socialist character of Islam. Inspired by them, lawmakers can develop economic theories suited to the age and keeping pace with the course of development. The overall spirit of Islam seeks social justice. In achieving it lie the welfare of humanity and the flourishing of civilisation. Ibn Khaldun says:
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00599

“Since injustice threatens the very survival of humanity through the destruction of civilisation that it brings about, the wisdom of prohibiting it is clear. Its prohibition is therefore important, and the evidence for it in the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet is too abundant to be listed and counted exhaustively.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00600
Once again, Ibn Khaldun puts his finger on one of the foundations of scientific socialism. He grasped the essence of what is known as “surplus value”. Here are his words:
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00601

“Among the worst forms of injustice, and the most destructive to civilisation, are the imposition of forced labour and the wrongful exploitation of the people. Labour is a form of wealth, for a person's livelihood and earnings are the value of the work that people perform in society. All their efforts and labour are thus wealth and earnings for them; indeed, they have no other earnings. The people who work to build up civilisation derive their living and their income from that very work. If they are forced to labour at tasks that are not their own, and made to serve others without pay in the work by which they earn their living, their earnings vanish and the value of their labour — their wealth — is taken from them. They suffer harm and lose a large share of their livelihood, or indeed their livelihood altogether. If this happens repeatedly, their hopes of improving civilisation are ruined. They cease to strive for it altogether, and civilisation falls into decline and ruin.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00602

My last point of disagreement with Abd al-Mughni Sa'id concerns history in the Quran. I will not go into Smith's comparison between the Islamic approach, with its material and spiritual aspects, and historical materialism, with its materialist outlook. Historical materialism has already been studied exhaustively. I refer the reader to Plekhanov's The Development of the Monist View of History. I will simply shed some light on the Quran's understanding of history and on the extent to which Muslim historians applied it in their own historical works.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00603

There is no dispute that history, as presented in the Quran, is meant to teach and guide us. This is clear from its many stories of the prophets and messengers, and from its accounts of vanished societies such as Ad and Thamud — what are known as the “tales of the ancients”. The Quran recounts all this for a moral purpose, in keeping with the reasons for its revelation. God says: “Travel through the land and see what became of the wrongdoers.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00604

The Quran's stories bring out God's power to create, His greatness in governing the universe and His knowledge of what was and what will be. But they also show us that human beings are free in their actions and have control over their own will. That is why people are responsible for their deeds: the reward or punishment is of the same nature as the deed itself. Human beings, as individuals and as communities, are therefore the makers of history. There is no contradiction here between the power of the Creator and people's creation of their own actions, or their complete freedom to shape the reality in which they live. Our deeds in this life are the gateway to the next: “Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00605

The point is that history is made by human beings, and their deeds are the historian's material. Anything beyond that lies outside the scope of historical research. Spiritual matters cannot be investigated by reason: “Say: the spirit is a matter for my Lord, and you have been given only a little knowledge.” The believer accepts these matters as matters of faith: “Those who believe in the unseen, perform the prayer, and give from what We have provided for them.” To delve into them is futile and dangerous. Ibn Khaldun warned against this when he said: “In the study of divine matters, there is no room for broadening speculation or multiplying questions.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00606

The Quran therefore urges people to exercise reason and unleash its powers in studying the phenomena of the universe that lie within its reach. We can discover their causes and the factors that bring them about without calling their first cause into question in the slightest. On the contrary, searching for and examining the causes of things deepens and strengthens faith. God says: “It is those of His servants who have knowledge who truly stand in awe of God.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00607

From the historical stories of the Quran we can therefore draw scientific guidance for historical research. Its basis is to set aside matters of the unseen and use reason to study what we can understand: to discover the nature of things, their causes and the laws governing their development. We can go further still. The lessons contained in the Quran's stories show us that it is possible to look ahead to the future — a distinctive feature of modern science. By examining the “tales of the ancients”, we can discern a law of inevitability in the common fate of states founded on injustice and tyranny.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00608

Yet the fact remains that the Islamic school of history before Ibn Khaldun did not follow this scientific approach. Historians understood the historical stories in the Quran as history itself. They did not dare explain events and occurrences, because they saw them as a fate already written. They were content to recount events and reports passed down from one generation to the next, on the assumption that history was a branch of knowledge received through tradition. Few applied reason to what had been handed down to them. Even then, they did so in a limited way, confining themselves to examining the accounts of those from whom they drew their information on the basis of how trustworthy the people reporting them were. They borrowed this practice from the scholars of the Prophet's sayings. It is well known that the beginnings of Islamic historical scholarship were bound up with the study of those sayings. It is a mistake to regard people who worked on history in those days as “historians”; a more accurate name for them is chroniclers. Scholars in other fields looked down upon them and treated their subject with contempt, considering it little more than “the telling of stories and the recounting of reports, the limits of its knowledge being anecdotes and evening tales”. Ibn Khaldun was right to say that the great Muslim historians had gathered the accounts of past times, only for interlopers to mix them with falsehoods they imagined and invented, embellishing them with unreliable stories they fabricated. They failed to observe or take account of the causes of events and circumstances. Careful investigation was rare; error and illusion were the close companions of these accounts. In fairness, we should acknowledge the efforts of some of the early historians, such as al-Tabari, al-Masudi and Miskawayh. But, as Ibn Khaldun says, they were “so few that one could almost count them on one's fingers”.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00609

It was Ibn Khaldun who transformed the methods of historical research in Islam. He was unquestionably the thinker who gave the field its theoretical foundations. One scholar described him as “the world's first philosopher of history”, and that is no exaggeration. Ibn Khaldun's thinking did not spring out of nowhere. I am convinced that he drew it from the Quran, which honoured reason and freed it from its chains. Its verses on this subject are too numerous to count: “Will you not see?” “Will you not look?” “Will you not reason?” And so on. If the Mu'tazilites deserve the credit for bringing reason to the study of faith, Ibn Khaldun pioneered a reasoned understanding of history. For him, history meant “careful reflection, investigation and explanation of things and their origins, and a deep knowledge of how events occur and what causes them”. There is so much to say about Ibn Khaldun , and extensive studies have been devoted to him. It will suffice here to quote Alban Widgery: “Ibn Khaldun is the founder of the science of history because he saw it as a distinct branch of knowledge, concerned with the whole range of social phenomena that make up actual history, revealing the various influences at work within it and the continuing chains of causes and effects.” What Widgery calls the “continuing chains of causes and effects” in Ibn Khaldun's method means that our philosopher understood the nature of dialectics. That understanding is the cornerstone of historical materialism, which seeks to identify the laws of historical change. With its help, we can explain the events of the past, establish the facts of the present and anticipate the direction of the future.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00610

In this regard Ibn Khaldun says: “I devised it as a remarkable approach among the various methods, an original way and a new style... so that you may understand the circumstances of the times and generations before you, and those that come after you.”
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00611

In short, the Quran contains general principles, not specific theories or methods cast in a rigid mould. Guided by those principles, lawmakers can develop coherent theories of politics and economics, and researchers can draw inspiration from them to develop a sound scientific approach to history.
A Modern Approach Strengthens Authenticity Rather Than Undermining It
passage-en-00612

If a historian and philosopher such as Ibn Khaldun was able to give history a clear form without in the least diminishing the exalted standing of the Quran, then modern historians ought to carry his work forward, drawing on the advances made in our own age. The miraculous nature of the Quran lies in the fact that it does not conflict with scientific progress, so long as its aim is human happiness and the good of humanity.

I followed with keen interest the debate between Dr Mahmoud Ismail and Ahmad Musa Salim on the subject of secret political movements in Islam. I was astonished that Dr Ismail should set aside the very principles of research in a study of such importance. He takes the claims of Bandali Jawzi and others like him as established truths, without troubling himself to undertake the careful investigation that intellectual honesty demands — especially when the subject concerns the very foundations of our historical and cultural heritage.
Arab Thought Under False Accusation
passage-en-00616

One would have expected the doctor to establish the facts from trustworthy sources before rushing to explain them or adopting other people's explanations. If reliable sources failed him, the rules of scientific research required him to suspend judgement and refrain from interpretation. Instead, we saw him discard all the Arabic sources, which, despite their differences, agree on a view contrary to his own, and then appeal to the authority of people such as Bernard Lewis, Émile Masqueray and Percy Smith. As if these gentlemen from abroad had devoted themselves with perfect integrity to correcting the lies that virtually all Muslim scholars and historians had conspired to tell! He did not stop for a moment to ask himself: what comes next, once we accuse our most distinguished Muslim scholars and historians, Shia and Sunni alike — al-Ghazali, al-Ash'ari, al-Shahrastani, Ibn Hazm, Ibn Taymiyya, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Fakhr al-Din al-Razi and many others — of conspiring to make up the claim that the Ismailis (the Batinis, or followers of hidden meanings) and the Qarmatians stood outside Islam rather than constituting schools of thought within it, as Dr Ismail maintains, following the views of certain Orientalists? Their aim, according to those scholars, was to abolish Islamic law in its entirety and deny the existence of the Creator; they believed in no religion and acknowledged no resurrection.
Arab Thought Under False Accusation
passage-en-00617

If all these scholars and historians conspired to lie and mislead us, then surely we ought to reject everything that has reached us through them: the Quran, the teachings and sayings of the Prophet, and the rest of our history. If we cannot trust them to tell the truth about the Ismailis and Qarmatians, how can we be sure they did not also agree to lie about our entire heritage, which has reached us only through them? To whom, then, shall we turn for knowledge of our religion and history? To Lewis, Émile and Smith?
Arab Thought Under False Accusation
passage-en-00618

An Arab who was keen to demolish the role of the Arabs in history — Dr Abd al-Rahman Badawi — has already written a book called The History of Atheism in Islam! In it he collected studies by Orientalists interested in the history of heresy in Islam, which, in Dr Badawi's view, represents the free current of the Arab spirit. But I wonder: was the work of Orientalists such as Goldziher, Heinrich Seder and Paul Kraus motivated purely by the pursuit of knowledge? And was that the sole motivation of these scholars and others like Margoliouth, O'Leary and Gauthier in their efforts to prove that the Arabs, because of their supposedly backward intellectual nature, were incapable of producing a civilisation or thought of any value? That everything they possessed, even the Quran itself, was borrowed from Hellenic (Greek) thought through the Syrians, Jews and Christians?
Arab Thought Under False Accusation
passage-en-00619

I do not mean by this to weigh up the merits and failings of Orientalist scholarship as a whole. A full assessment would reveal a valuable contribution, deserving our gratitude, from sincere scholars — and even some whose motives were less sincere — in uncovering the Arab-Islamic heritage and bringing its worth to light. We need to benefit from the positive side of Orientalist scholarship. But we must never take our religion from these scholars or come to understand our heritage through their minds! We are in desperate need of a fresh examination of our heritage, using Arab minds and a sound scientific method. Our heritage needs to be gathered together, organised and carefully checked. We need a way of establishing the reliability of historical accounts. We have before us the methods of the scholars of the Prophet's sayings, who assessed the trustworthiness of those who passed them down, and Ibn Khaldun's approach to history.
Arab Thought Under False Accusation
passage-en-00620

It is possible to correct our understanding of history and judge it in the light of the actual conditions of its time. But it will take painstaking work and a scientific approach whose requirements must be met in full. Only then will a picture of this history emerge that differs from those offered by traditional and modern scholars alike. Drawing on what I know of this history, I would like to outline a few ideas. I hope that Rose al-Yusuf will be open to a detailed discussion of them, thereby rendering a great service to the task of setting this history straight.
Arab Thought Under False Accusation
passage-en-00621

I believe such research will show that Arab society, both before and after Islam, was a classless society, unlike the structure of other societies. Nor did it know slavery in the form in which other societies knew it. We will see that the Arabs who went forth under the banner of Islam fought a sincere struggle — and I do not exclude the Umayyads or Abbasids — to free the societies whose states they overthrew from servitude to kings, priests and feudal landowners, and bring them into the service of the one God, under a system of justice and standards before whose revealed law everyone in society stood equal without discrimination. It will also become clear that the Arabs' exclusive hold on power was not an act of selfishness. It was a necessity dictated by what was right and by the common good, both because they were the guardians of this religion and because of the solidarity needed to uphold the authority of the state, establish justice and protect its borders, as Ibn Khaldun explains. Had the Arabs failed in this duty, those who resented the loss of their kingdoms would have risen against them — as they often tried to do. Islam would have become, if it were remembered at all, no more than a passing item in the historical record!
Arab Thought Under False Accusation
passage-en-00622

We will see that the bloody conflict among the Companions of the Messenger of God, which ended with the establishment of Umayyad rule, was not entirely what we imagine it to have been. It was not a struggle driven by aggression and injustice. Rather, it was a conflict between free, capable believers, each exercising their own judgement on a matter for which there was no explicit religious text: the form the state should take. In the end, the struggle was decided in favour of the person most capable of running the state, even if he was not the most distinguished in his early devotion to Islam, his struggle for it or his piety. Mu'awiya himself acknowledged this when he said: “People, I am not the best among you. There are people among you who are better than I am: Abd Allah ibn Umar, Abd Allah ibn Amr and other men of excellence. But perhaps I can be of the greatest benefit to you in governing, be the best at facing your enemy, and bring you the richest yield.”
Arab Thought Under False Accusation
passage-en-00623

Indeed, the study of the Arabic language and pre-Islamic poetry reveals a highly developed Arab civilisation before Islam, one that had arrived at the noblest and soundest understanding of God and of existence (the world), and at the most precise moral standard humanity had reached without divine revelation. In these fields, Arab thought was more advanced than Greek thought in its various schools, and than the schools influenced by it. The approach Arab thought had taken in building this civilisation was a sound scientific one, based on observing phenomena, classifying and organising them, and drawing conclusions. Islam's encounter with this thought was a struggle to correct and refine it, not to demolish and replace it. And Islam emerged from the Arabian Peninsula to wage a fierce struggle against pagan beliefs clothed in Hellenic philosophy, Indian myths and Persian heresies. Arab thought, strengthened by Islam, taught more than it learnt and fought to free humanity from empty argument, superstition and myth. It was a fierce struggle, with victories and losses. Arab thought built its second civilisation under Islam, and then its sun shone upon Europe, where it helped build a third civilisation through science, as the fair-minded German Orientalist “Siegfried” acknowledged after Europe had turned its back on it!
Arab Thought Under False Accusation

Finally, we will establish that the Ismaili and Qarmatian movements did not arise for the sake of justice, but to destroy Islam and Arab thought. And this brings us to a final question: was it merely a coincidence that the leader of the Ismaili movement was Maimun ibn Daysan ibn Sa'id the Jew, a descendant of al-Shal'la'? And that Jews are also the leaders of the modern Masonic movement? Was it a coincidence that both movements used secrecy, deception, fraud and degrees of initiation, killed elderly people, women, children and adults, and brought destruction? And that both movements had the same aim of destroying religions, especially Islam, and humiliating peoples, especially the Arabs?

passage-en-00625

The hatred of the Jews for Ishmael, who received his father's birthright instead of their forefather Isaac, and for the Arab descendants of Ishmael who inherited Abraham's blessing, has never subsided and will not subside until the descendants of Ishmael are humiliated and the kingdom of Israel is established on their land! Is it not time for us to wake up and take notice? I hope this will happen before it is too late.

Here is the text:
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00629

In the issue before last of Rose al-Yusuf, Rashad Khalil presented us with an article entitled “Arab Thought Under False Accusation”. It raises a number of questions about the Islamic heritage. Some concern Muslim thinkers and Orientalist scholarship. Others deal with broad issues such as the place of Arab civilisation in history, or specific matters such as the origins of the Ismailis. Beyond this, the article contains its author's own views and ideas about Arab society before and after Islam, and his interpretation of the question of the caliphate and the struggle over it in the early days of Islam.
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00630

The finger of accusation, on the charge of slandering Arab thought, points at the author of “Secret Political Movements in Islam”. And that author accuses the self-appointed guardians of Arab thought of precisely the same thing. Arab-Islamic thought is neither anyone's monopoly nor an estate to be passed down from one generation to the next. The reason for its present backwardness lies with those who have cut it off from the course of human intellectual development and surrounded it with walls of priestly authority. There is no need to point to their connections with the forces of domination and colonialism; that is a fact recorded in our modern and contemporary history. It is enough to recall how habitually they have brandished the sword of their own interests in the name of religion against anyone who sought to free Arab thought from their guardianship — from al-Afghani and Muhammad Abduh to Khalid Muhammad Khalid and Abd al-Rahman al-Sharqawi. It is these people whom I accuse of falsehood.
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00631
I must discuss Khalil's views on all the questions he has raised. Given their number and variety, I find myself obliged to refer the reader to certain works for further clarification.
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00632

The first point concerns Muslim thinkers and historians such as al-Ghazali, al-Ash'ari, al-Shahrastani, Ibn Hazm, Ibn Taymiyya, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, who denounced the Ismaili movement. To disagree with them on one particular subject is not to say that they conspired to lie and mislead us in everything they left behind. There were also Muslim thinkers who disagreed with them and refuted their claims about the Ismailis. Among them was Ibn Khaldun, whose method Khalil himself urged us to adopt.
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00633

The disagreements between historians of Islam arose from their religious affiliations, which in turn grew out of their social circumstances. All those who were biased against the Ismailis represented the traditionalist current in religious thought and, socially, belonged to the upper or at least the middle classes. Take al-Ash'ari, a descendant of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, one of the governors of Iraq in the early days of Islam. He broke away from the Mu'tazilites, the pioneers of rational thought, and laid the foundations of a traditionalist religious current that was politically reactionary, serving the Abbasids. Al-Ghazali strengthened this current and grew wealthier through his association with the Seljuk minister Nizam al-Mulk. It is well known that Ibn Hazm, Ibn Taymiyya and al-Shahrastani, all Sunnis, regarded the Sunni school as “the group destined for salvation” and all other groups as “doomed”.*
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00634

This traditionalist current gained ground until it overwhelmed the rational approach that had begun with the Mu'tazilites and ended with Ibn Rushd. Traditionalism reached its peak in the hands of Sufis such as Ibn Arabi and Ibn Sab'in. Little by little, the voice of reason faded, until it was drowned out by the clamour of unthinking dervish devotion, which weighed heavily on Islamic thought.
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00635

As for al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, they wrote their histories in the Abbasid age, when the descendants of Ali suffered even greater hardship and persecution than they had under the Umayyads. One of their poets went so far as to say:
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00637
Would that the tyranny of the sons of Marwan might return to us! Would that the justice of the Abbasids might burn in hell!
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00638
That is why historians did not dare do justice to the Ismaili movements that opposed the Abbasid caliphate.**
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00639

Linked to this point is the accusation that we ignored the original sources and drew instead on Orientalists such as Jawzi, Smith, Masqueray and Lewis. A glance at what we wrote about Masqueray and Smith will show that we merely acknowledged their efforts to uncover works from our heritage dealing with the Kharijites. We did not borrow a single opinion from either of them. As for Jawzi, we dealt with the claim that we borrowed from him in a previous article. And no fair-minded researcher can call into question the objectivity of the modern historian Bernard Lewis, under whom some of our finest contemporary historians of Islam studied.
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00640

As for Seder and Kraus, we made no reference to either of them whatsoever, directly or indirectly. The same is true of Goldziher. Indeed, in a study of ours entitled On Islamic Thought, we disagreed with his views on the study of the Prophet's sayings and Gnosticism. In that same study we examined O'Leary's views on Islamic mysticism and rejected them, as we did Grégoire's views linking Islamic beliefs with Hellenism. No one denies the contribution of Orientalist scholarship to our heritage — something Khalil himself has acknowledged — so there is no need to dwell on it. But there is a question I would like to put to Khalil, the librarian of the world's largest Islamic university: what has he contributed to the study of our heritage in the way of bibliographical work? Perhaps he feels a little ashamed when he sees the monumental work produced by a colleague of his at the British Museum named Pearson, whose Index Islamicus brought together Islamic studies and periodical publications from scholarly journals around the world. Surely Khalil would be better serving Arab thought by doing work of this kind, rather than uttering resounding words and hollow speeches from the pulpit!
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00641

The next point concerns his hazy, utopian picture of Arab society: “Arab society before and after Islam was classless, unlike the structure of other societies.” In reality, pre-Islamic nomadic society saw class conflict over water and pasture, a phenomenon recorded in literary works in the accounts known as the “Days of the Arabs”. If the struggle took the outward form of tribal conflict, it was because the tribe was the backbone of the social system. This also explains the existence of tribal alliances: smaller tribes banded together to resist the domination of more powerful ones. In urban society, with its more developed political system, class conflict stood out in sharp relief. Consider a city like Mecca: at the top of its social pyramid stood the wealthy merchant class, and at the bottom were enslaved workers of Persian, Byzantine, Ethiopian and other origins. What a gulf separated the position of a man like Abu Sufyan from that of a man like Bilal, who called the faithful to prayer for the Prophet!*
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00642

When Islam appeared, the oppressed classes of slaves and mawali formed its ranks against the wealthy merchants, who saw Islam as a threat to their interests. The triumph of Islam struck a blow at a class system founded on wealth and ancestry. Piety became the measure of distinction between one Muslim and another. Muslim society enjoyed social justice in the time of the Prophet and his first two successors. Under Uthman, a new aristocracy of leading Companions, such as Talha, al-Zubayr and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, reasserted itself, taking advantage of Uthman's weakness and advanced age. Ali ibn Abi Talib took up the cause of the oppressed classes. The struggle between all these forces eventually ended in the triumph of the aristocracy of Abu Sufyan's family.
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00643
In short, despite its outwardly political and religious character, the struggle over the caliphate was first and foremost a class struggle, not a difference of judgement over an uncertain question.**
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00644

The next point concerns Khalil's exaggerated assessment of the standing of Arab civilisation before Islam. What conceivable reasoning could justify his claim that “Arab thought before Islam was more advanced than Greek thought in its various schools and the schools influenced by it”?
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00645
I hardly think I need to comment!
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00646

The greatness of Islamic civilisation stems from its openness to human thought, both Eastern and Western, free from prejudice or rigidity. It translated that thought, made it its own and added to it. In doing so, it enriched world civilisation, both by preserving classical thought and by developing it and presenting it in an Islamic form. The place of Islamic civilisation in history becomes clear when we see what it drew from those that came before it and what it gave to those that followed.*
Who Is Really Making False Accusations?
passage-en-00647

The last point of disagreement concerns his portrayal of the Ismaili movement as “a counter-revolution carefully planned by Jews out of hatred for Ishmael, who received his father's birthright instead of their forefather Isaac”, and his claim that the role of Maimun ibn Sa'id ibn Daysan in the Ismaili movement casts doubt on its true nature. Arab scholars and Orientalists have already examined this subject exhaustively. They concluded that the attempts to discredit the Ismaili movement originated with its Abbasid enemies. I will confine myself here to the words of Ibn Khaldun:

passage-en-00648

“Among the unreliable reports is the view taken by many historians and supposedly reliable authorities regarding the Ubaydids, the Shia caliphs of Kairouan and Cairo, denying their descent from the family of the Prophet (may God's blessings be upon them) and casting aspersions on their lineage... They rely on accounts fabricated for the weaker Abbasid caliphs, in order to curry favour with them by disparaging those who opposed them and inventing suspicions about their enemies.”**
